findings: Independent sources confirm the identification as Broad-winged Hawk, Buteo platypterus, family Accipitridae. The primary specimen and reference photographs agree in compact build, large head, short square tail, and adult light-morph plumage.
The measurements are correct: length 34–44 cm (13.4–17.3 in), wingspan 81–100 cm (31.9–39.4 in), and weight 265–560 g (9.3–19.8 oz).

All visible measurement graphics are internally consistent. The body-length ruler rises from 34 cm to 44 cm, has exactly four evenly spaced unlabeled interior ticks, repeats the correct range separately, and is explicitly marked “SCHEMATIC – NOT TO SCALE.”

The adult specimen correctly shows a reddish-brown head, brown to dark-brown upperparts, pale underparts with horizontal chestnut barring, and a strongly black-and-white-banded tail. The field-mark wording distinguishing the reddish head from the browner upperparts is supported by the sources.

The detached underwing study correctly depicts a broad, slightly pointed wing with a pale underside and dark trailing border. Its separation and labeling make it clearly supplementary rather than an extra attached wing.

The primary specimen contains exactly one head, one bill, two wings, two legs, and one tail. Both legs terminate in plausible anisodactyl raptor feet gripping the branch, with yellow tarsi and dark curved talons.

In both depicted heads, the upper and lower mandibles can be traced independently from their shared base. The hooked upper mandible projects beyond the lower in the correct direction and by a consistent, plausible amount; neither bill is co-terminal, reversed, truncated, or materially inconsistent with the side-profile references.
The eye, yellow cere, hooked dark bill, yellow legs, stocky proportions, folded-wing length, and tail configuration are consistent with Broad-winged Hawk anatomy and the supplied field photographs.

The habitat text is supported by the live sources: breeding birds use large deciduous or mixed forests, commonly near openings or water, while migrants and wintering birds also use forest edges, tropical or cloud forest, and arid scrub.

The behavior and diet text is supported: the species is diurnal, hunts from perches by dropping or swooping onto prey, consumes mammals, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and insects, is generally solitary and territorial outside migration, and forms large soaring migration kettles using thermals.
The juvenile description is accurate: juveniles are paler below with coarse longitudinal brown streaking and do not share the adult’s bold tail pattern.

Every visible name, heading, label, numerical value, unit, habitat statement, behavior statement, and field-mark line is legible and scientifically coherent. No duplicated, omitted, substituted, or nonsensical text requiring correction was found.
The palette swatches appropriately represent reddish brown, chestnut, cream white, charcoal black, and golden yellow without introducing additional factual claims.
The layout is balanced and readable, with the primary specimen dominant and the supplementary underwing, magnified head, palette, and schematic ruler clearly separated.
No place name, ZIP code, coordinates, map, or local-observation detail appears.
